name: Olympians
note: The twelve of the mountain, and their children

Hestia.name: Hestia (Vesta)
Hestia.note: The hearth, eldest of the six and the one who never left it -- she swore by Zeus' head to stay a virgin and keeps the fire at the centre of every house and city. Roman: Vesta, whose Vestal Virgins kept Rome's public fire, and whose name gives the vesta, an old word for a match. Theog. 454

Demeter.name: Demeter (Ceres)
Demeter.note: Grain and the harvest, who let the whole earth go barren while she looked for her daughter. Roman: Ceres -- and cereal is her name directly. Theog. 454, Hom. Hymn Dem.

Hera.name: Hera (Juno)
Hera.note: Queen of the gods, wife and sister of Zeus, and the implacable enemy of every woman he touched and every child they bore. Roman: Juno, from whom June is named, and Juno Moneta whose temple gives money. Theog. 454, Il. passim

Haides.name: Haides (Pluto)
Haides.note: The unseen one -- the name means invisible, and men avoided saying it, calling him Plouton, the rich, instead, because everything that grows comes up out of the ground. Roman: Pluto, Dis Pater. Gives plutocracy from the same root of wealth, and plutonium, named in 1941 after the planet, which was named after him. Theog. 455

Poseidon.name: Poseidon (Neptune)
Poseidon.note: Earth-shaker and lord of the sea, of horses and of earthquakes. Roman: Neptune -- and neptunium, element 93, named for the planet beyond Uranus exactly as plutonium was for the one beyond that. Theog. 456 He loved Pelops and gave him the winged chariot that won Hippodameia -- the race that founded the house of Atreus.

Zeus.name: Zeus (Jupiter)
Zeus.note: The last-born and the one who won: he made Kronos vomit up his brothers and sisters and led them ten years against the Titans. Roman: Jupiter -- Iu-piter, 'sky father', which is the SAME WORD, root and all, as Sanskrit Dyaus Pita, the sky father of the Rig Veda who stands at the top of the Hiranyagarbha tree. Zeus, Jupiter, Dyaus and the Latin deus and dies all descend from one Indo-European word for the bright daylit sky. Gives jovial, from Jupiter's astrological temper, and by Jove. Theog. 457, 468-500

Athena.name: Athena (Minerva)
Athena.note: Born from Zeus' head, full-grown and armed, after he swallowed her mother Metis: no womb, no childhood. Goddess of war fought with the mind, and of the crafts. Roman: Minerva. Athens is named for her, or she for it. Theog. 886-900, 924-926

Horai.name: Horai (Horae)
Horai.note: The Seasons -- Eunomia (good order), Dike (justice) and Eirene (peace): the three things that make a city's year work. Gives hour, and horology. Theog. 901-903

Charites.name: Charites (Gratiae)
Charites.note: The three Graces -- Aglaia, Euphrosyne, Thalia: splendour, good cheer, festivity. Roman: Gratiae, which gives grace, gracious, gratitude, gratis and grateful. Theog. 907-911

Persephone.name: Persephone (Proserpina)
Persephone.note: Carried off by Haides while picking flowers, and bound to the underworld for a third of every year by the six pomegranate seeds she ate there. Roman: Proserpina. Her going down and coming up is the winter and the spring. Theog. 912-914, Hom. Hymn Dem. She and Aphrodite both claimed Adonis, and Zeus divided his year between them.

Mousai.name: Mousai (Camenae)
Mousai.note: The nine: Kalliope, Kleio, Euterpe, Thaleia, Melpomene, Terpsichore, Erato, Polymnia, Ourania. Roman: Camenae. Their name gives music, museum (a seat of the Muses), mosaic and amuse. Theog. 915-917, 75-79

Apollon.name: Apollon (Apollo)
Apollon.note: Light, prophecy, music, plague and healing at once -- he shoots the arrows of sickness and takes them away. His oracle at Delphi ruled Greek politics for centuries. Roman: Apollo, the one major god the Romans took without renaming. Gives Apollonian, the ordered against the Dionysian. Theog. 918-920, Hom. Hymn Ap. His loves ran both ways and almost all of them ended badly: Daphne became the laurel rather than be caught, Kassandra took his gift and refused him, Koronis was unfaithful, and Hyakinthos and Kyparissos both died and became plants.

Artemis.name: Artemis (Diana)
Artemis.note: The hunt, wild country, and childbirth; she asked Zeus for eternal virginity and a bow at three years old. Roman: Diana. Her temple at Ephesos was one of the seven wonders. Theog. 918-920

Ares.name: Ares (Mars)
Ares.note: War as slaughter and noise -- Zeus tells him to his face he is the most hateful of the gods. Roman: MARS, who is a far greater figure at Rome than Ares ever was in Greece: father of Romulus, guardian of the fields, and the god the Romans thought they descended from. Gives martial, court-martial, March (his month, when campaigning resumed), and Tuesday by way of the Norse Tiw, whom the Romans matched to him. Theog. 921-923

Hebe.name: Hebe (Juventas)
Hebe.note: Youth, who poured the gods' nectar until she married Herakles when he was made a god. Roman: Juventas. Gives ephebe, and hebephrenia. Theog. 921-923

Eileithyia.note: Goddess of childbirth, who can hold a labour back or let it come. Theog. 921-923

Hephaistos.name: Hephaistos (Vulcan)
Hephaistos.note: The smith, and the only ugly god and the only lame one. Hera bore him alone, out of spite at Athena's birth, and threw him off Olympos for his lameness. Roman: VULCAN -- whose name gives volcano (his forge under Aitna) and vulcanise, Goodyear's 1844 process for hardening rubber with heat. Theog. 924-929

Aphrodite.name: Aphrodite (Venus)
Aphrodite.note: Born of the foam -- aphros -- where Ouranos' severed parts fell into the sea off Kythera, which makes her older than Zeus and no child of his. Homer instead calls her daughter of Zeus and Dione, and both traditions are ancient; this tree draws Hesiod's and records Homer's. Roman: Venus -- venereal, venerate, and Friday, dies Veneris, which is Freitag and vendredi still. Gives aphrodisiac. Theog. 188-206; cf. Il. 5.370-371

Erinyes.name: Erinyes (Furiae)
Erinyes.note: The Furies -- Alekto, Megaira, Tisiphone -- born from the blood of the same wound that fell on the earth. They hunt kin-murderers and cannot be called off; the Greeks called them the Kindly Ones to avoid naming them. Roman: Furiae, Dirae. Gives megaera, and fury. Theog. 183-185

Gigantes.note: The Giants, sprung from Ouranos' blood in armour, who piled mountains at Olympos and were put down only because a mortal, Herakles, fought on the gods' side as prophecy required. Gives giant, gigantic. Theog. 185-186

Meliai.note: The ash-tree nymphs, born from the same blood. Theog. 187

Eros2.name: Eros (Cupid)
Eros2.note: The winged boy with the bow, son of Ares and Aphrodite -- distinct from primordial Eros above, and the one who marries Psyche. Roman: Cupid, whence cupidity. Theog. 933-937; Apuleius

Phobos.note: Fear or rout, who drives his father's chariot. Gives phobia, and the inner moon of Mars. Theog. 934

Deimos.note: Terror, his brother; the outer moon of Mars. Theog. 934

Dionysos.name: Dionysos (Bacchus)
Dionysos.note: Twice-born: once from Semele and once from Zeus' thigh. Wine, theatre, and the loss of self -- the youngest Olympian and the only one with a mortal mother, which is why he stands here in the Theban generation rather than up among the others. Roman: BACCHUS, or Liber. Gives bacchanal, bacchant, and the Dionysian against the Apollonian. Apollod. 3.4.3, 3.5.1-3

Hermes.name: Hermes (Mercury)
Hermes.note: Born at dawn, played the lyre by midday and stole Apollo's cattle by evening. God of roads, traders, thieves, heralds and the boundary stone; the one who takes souls down. Roman: MERCURY, from merx, merchandise -- whence merchant, commerce, and the element mercury, quicksilver, for its speed. Gives hermetic (from Hermes Trismegistos and the sealed vessels of alchemy) and hermeneutics, the art of interpreting. Hom. Hymn Herm.

Hermaphroditos.note: Son of Hermes and Aphrodite, and named from both. The nymph Salmakis embraced him in her pool and prayed never to be parted, and the gods took her literally: the two became one body of both sexes. HERMAPHRODITE. Ov. Met. 4.285-388

unions.note: Kronos swallowed each of them at birth, having heard he would be put down by his own son; Rheia bore Zeus in Crete and gave her husband a stone in swaddling clothes. The order here is birth order, and Zeus is both youngest and, having disgorged the rest, eldest. Theog. 453-500
Zeus' first marriage, ended by his eating his wife. Theog. 886-900

Carried off through a split in the field while she was picking flowers, with her father's consent and not her own, and married to him below: queen of the dead, bound to return for a third of every year by the six pomegranate seeds she ate there. Hom. Hymn Dem. 1-89
Without any act of love, in anger at Zeus for producing Athena from his own head: answering a motherless birth with a fatherless one. Theog. 924-929

Kronos threw the parts he cut from his father into the sea, and a white foam spread from the immortal flesh, and in it a girl grew. A one-parent union: there is no mother, which is exactly what the sources say. Theog. 188-200
The drops that fell on Gaia rather than into the sea. Theog. 183-187
Helios saw them and told Hephaistos, who trapped them in a net of chains finer than a spider's and called the gods in to laugh. Od. 8.266-366; Theog. 933-937
Ov. Met. 4.288
He came to her wearing Artemis' own shape, which is how he got near a huntress sworn to Artemis. She was turned into a bear for it. Apollod. 3.8.2
He grieved for a tame stag until he asked to mourn for ever, and became the cypress. Ov. Met. 10.106-142
He watched her wrestle a lion bare-handed, asked Cheiron who she was, and carried her to Libya. Pind. Pyth. 9
Killed by a discus in the same way, and from his blood the crocus, and saffron from that. Ov. Fasti 5.227
He put her to sleep first, and Apollo came the same night in an old woman's shape. Ov. Met. 11.301-317
Mother of Pan. Hom. Hymn Pan 33-39
He came to her wearing the shape of the river Enipeus, whom she loved. Od. 11.235-259
A satyr youth, killed by a wild bull and turned into the first grapevine. Nonnus 10-12
She and Persephone both claimed him, and Zeus divided his year between them. Apollod. 3.14.4
Her share of the year, which is the other half of the same quarrel. Apollod. 3.14.4
After the pyre on Oite: made immortal and married to Youth herself, which is the reconciliation with the goddess whose name he carried all his life. Theog. 950-955
